# Abstract

Between 1914 and 1926 the towns of the former Russian Empire went through two sharp upheavals. First World War evacuations emptied the western borderland cities of Riga, Liepaja, Kovno, Vilna and Warsaw while crowding rear garrison and railway towns in the interior; then food and fuel shortages under War Communism cut Petrograd by 70,2% and Moscow by nearly half between 1917 and 1920 before the New Economic Policy (*NEP*) and post-war refugee returns restored urban trade and industry. This gazetteer presents population figures for 8.053 urban and census-enumerated settlements across the 48 pre-war provinces (18,61M km2) between 1914 and 1926.

# Methodology

The settlement series are drawn from the 1914 Russian statistical yearbooks, the 1917 town census [@vseros1917gorod], the 28 August 1920 Russian census [@tsu1920perepis], the 1920 Finnish census [@svt1923finland], the 1920 and 1925 Latvian censuses [@skujenieks1927latvia], the 30 September 1921 Polish census [@gus1921skorowidz; @barwinski2015ethnic], the 15 February 1921 Czechoslovak census [@csr1924scitani], the 28 December 1922 Estonian census [@estonia1924rahvaloendus], the 17 September 1923 Lithuanian census [@lithuania1926gyventojai], Romanian municipal counts for Bessarabia and Bukovina [@tartakovsky2009bessarabia; @fondos2024bessarabia], the 15 March 1923 Soviet urban census [@tsu1923gorod] and the 17 December 1926 All-Union Census [@tsu1926vsesoyuznaya; @koenker1985urbanization; @volkov1930dinamika].



# Results

## Regions 1 - 4: Former Congress Poland

Table \ref{tab:reg1-4} gives population figures for 220 settlements across Warsaw, Plock and Lomza (Region 1), Piotrkow and Kalisz (Region 2), Lublin, Siedlce and Kholm (Region 3) and Radom, Kielce and Suwalki (Region 4) [@gus1921skorowidz; @barwinski2015ethnic; @gatrell1999whole].
